opus-5.5.text:
For me it really starts with meeting scientists where they already are. Researchers don't want another standalone tool they have to log into, learn from scratch, and then copy results out of. They have their own rhythms: reading papers, designing experiments, running assays, analyzing data, going back to the literature when something surprising comes up. So the question I keep asking is, where in that loop does a model actually remove friction or open up something new, rather than just adding a step?

In practice, a lot of the value shows up in pretty unglamorous places. Helping someone get through a huge body of literature and pull out the threads that matter for their specific question. Helping write or debug the analysis code for a messy dataset. Working out an experimental design, or thinking through controls they might have missed. Those are things every lab does constantly, and if a model can do them well inside the tools people already use, that compounds over time.

The other piece is trust. Scientists are, rightly, skeptical people. So the model has to be transparent about its reasoning, point back to sources, and be honest about uncertainty. In biology especially, a confident wrong answer can send someone down a path that costs months at the bench. So we think a lot about how to make the model a good collaborator: one that proposes hypotheses and does the heavy lifting on analysis, but leaves the scientist firmly in the loop for judgment calls and validation.

And finally, it has to be a two-way relationship. The most useful thing we can do is work closely with actual researchers, watch where the model helps and where it falls short, and feed that back into improving it. The goal isn't to replace the scientist. It's to give every researcher something like a tireless, very well-read lab partner, so they can spend more of their time on the creative, high-judgment parts of science that got them into the field in the first place.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the model isn't the product, the workflow is. A scientist doesn't wake up wanting to query a protein language model. They wake up with a hypothesis, a half-finished experiment, and a pile of data that doesn't quite make sense. If the model shows up as a separate tool they have to leave their world to use, it mostly won't get used, no matter how good the benchmark numbers are.

So the first thing we do is go sit with the researchers and watch what they actually do. Where do they spend their hours? Often it's not the glamorous part. It's cleaning assay data, reading forty papers to figure out whether a target is worth pursuing, designing the next round of constructs, writing up results for a committee. Those are the moments where a model can quietly take work off their plate. We try to meet them inside the notebook, the electronic lab notebook, the analysis pipeline they already run, rather than asking them to come to us.

The second thing is trust, and in life sciences that's earned differently than in, say, coding. If a model suggests a sequence edit or a candidate compound, the scientist needs to be able to see why. What evidence pointed there? What's the confidence? What would falsify it? We design for that interrogation. A prediction with no provenance is a dead end for a careful biologist, and honestly it should be.

The third thing is the feedback loop. The beautiful part of embedding in the workflow is that the experiment itself becomes the evaluation. The model proposes, the lab tests, the result comes back, and that's signal you can learn from. If you build it right, the model gets better at the specific problems that lab cares about, instead of just being broadly competent and locally mediocre.

And I'd add one caution. It's tempting to automate the whole pipeline end to end. I think the right posture right now is a collaborator, not an autopilot. Let the scientist steer, let the model expand the space of what they can consider and how fast they can move through it. The teams that get the most out of these tools treat them as a very fast, very well-read colleague who still has to show their work.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the researcher’s workflow and the scientific question they’re trying to answer. Where are they spending time translating between tools, searching through information, or trying to make sense of a result? Those are places where a model could help, provided it fits into how they already work.

And the right interface might not always be a chat window. It could be a capability inside an analysis tool that helps someone interpret an output, examine alternative explanations, or decide what experiment to run next. The researcher needs to be able to inspect the evidence, understand the limitations, and challenge the suggestion.

For me, the measure of success is whether it helps researchers do better science. Does it help them ask a sharper question or get to an informative experiment sooner? That’s what should guide how we build it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the researcher’s workflow and the question they’re trying to answer. Where are they spending time? Where are they getting stuck? And where could a model help them make a better decision about what to do next?

In life sciences, generating an answer is only part of the work. A researcher needs to understand the evidence behind it, the assumptions, and the uncertainty. So I’d want the model to help them move between the literature, their data, and possible experiments, while making it easy to inspect and challenge its suggestions.

And that should be an iterative loop: you form a hypothesis, design an experiment, get results, and update your thinking. The opportunity is to support that whole loop in the tools researchers already use. Ultimately, success means helping them get to a useful, testable insight faster.
